pulls.title: refactor: Add util::Result failure types and ability to merge result values
pulls.body:
Add `util::Result` support for returning more error information and make use of it in [LoadChainstate method](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25665/commits/b1c0feb6656befc48a6840c1d841074bd6131b78) as an initial application. Followup PRs [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) and [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) use it more broadly to return errors and warnings from wallet and kernel functions as well.

This change adds two major features to the result class:

- For better error handling, adds the ability to return a value on failure, not just a value on success. This is a key missing feature that makes the result class not useful for functions like `LoadChainstate()` which produce different errors that need to be handled differently [^1].

[^1]: Ability to return error values was actually present in the original implementation of [#25218](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25218), but unfortunately removed in later iterations. See [design notes](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/bitcoin-devwiki/wiki/util::Result-design-notes).

- For better error reporting, adds the ability to return warning messages and multiple errors, not just a single error string. This provides a way for functions to report errors and warnings in a standard way, and simplifies interfaces:

    ```diff
    -virtual std::unique_ptr<Wallet> loadWallet(const std::string& name, bilingual_str& error, std::vector<bilingual_str>& warnings) = 0;
    +virtual util::Result<std::unique_ptr<Wallet>> loadWallet(const std::string& name) = 0;
    ```

    ```diff
    -std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options, DatabaseStatus& status, bilingual_str& error);
    +util::Result<std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase>, DatabaseError> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options);
   ```

This change also makes some more minor improvements:

- Smaller type size. `util::Result<int>` is 16 bytes, and `util::Result<void>` is 8 bytes. Previously both were 72 bytes.

- Broader type compatibility. Supports noncopyable and nonmovable success and error types.

### Comparison with `std::expected`

Currently, the `util::Result` class is useful for error reporting—returning translated, user-facing error strings—but not as useful for error handling, where callers need structured failure information to decide how to proceed. By contrast, `std::expected` / `util::Expected` (#34005, #34006) is good for error handling but less helpful for reporting. This PR closes the gap between the two classes.

With this PR, `std::expected` remains a good choice for lower-level functions or simple functions that fail in only a few well-defined ways. Meanwhile,

- `Result` becomes a better choice for operations that can fail in many different ways—loading a wallet, connecting a block, etc.—where callers may want complete error traces, not just low-level errors without context or high-level errors without detail. (Followup [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) applies this to wallet-loading functions.) 
- `Result` can also be more useful than `expected` when merging status information from multiple calls. (Followup [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) uses this to reliably propagate flush and fatal-error status from validation code that can internally trigger flushes or shutdowns.)
- `Result` may also be a better choice than `std::expected` when returning pointer values. (Followup [#26022](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022) adds a `ResultPtr` specialization that avoids double dereferencing.) 
- `Result` can be more efficient than `std::expected` when failures are rare but failure objects are large, since failure values are heap-allocated.

This PR effectively makes `Result` a superset of `expected`, making the representations compatible and allowing them to be used together.

pulls.title: Add util::ResultPtr class
pulls.body:
<!-- begin based-on -->
**This is based on #25665.** The non-base commits are:

- [`3d008913cdb` Add util::ResultPtr class](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/3d008913cdb697651e67cd5ee158cc12a9611c0e)
- [`2d0915656c8` Use ResultPtr<unique_ptr> instead of Result<unique_ptr>](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/2d0915656c80d45642965b1963f158d865846f5b)<!-- end -->

---

The `util::ResultPtr` class is a wrapper for `util::Result` providing syntax sugar to make it less awkward to use with returned pointers. Instead of needing to be deferenced twice with `**result` or `(*result)->member`, it only needs to be dereferenced once with `*result` or `result->member`. Also when it is used in a boolean context, instead of evaluating to true when there is no error and the pointer is null, it evaluates to false so it is straightforward to determine whether the result points to something.

This PR is only partial a solution to #26004 because while it makes it easier to check for null pointer values, it does not make it impossible to return a null pointer value inside a successful result. It would be possible to enforce that successful results always contain non-null pointers by using a `not_null` type (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/24423) in combination with `ResultPtr`, though.

pulls.title: wallet: Track no-longer-spendable TXOs separately
pulls.body:
In #27286, the wallet keeps track of all of its transaction outputs, even if they are already spent or are otherwise unspendable. This TXO set is iterated for balance checking and coin selection preparation, which can still be slow for wallets that have had a lot of activity. This PR aims to improve the performance of such wallets by moving UTXOs that are definitely no longer spendable to a different map in the wallet so that far fewer TXOs need to be iterated for the aforementioned functions.

Unspendable TXOs (not to be confused with Unspent TXOs) are those which have a spending transaction that has been confirmed, or are no longer valid due to reorgs. TXOs that are spent in unconfirmed transactions remain in the primary TXO set, and are filtered out of balance and coin selection as before.

pulls.title: log, refactor: Allow log macros to accept context arguments
pulls.body:
Allow `LogTrace()`, `LogDebug()`, `LogInfo()`, `LogWarning()`, and `LogError()` macros to accept context arguments to provide more information in log messages and more control over logging to callers.

For example, with this change wallet code can log with (in #30343):

```diff
-        WalletLogPrintf("Error: cannot erase address book entry data\n");
+        LogError(m_log, "Error: cannot erase address book entry data\n");
```

And kernel code can log with (in #30342):

```diff
-        LogDebug(BCLog::VALIDATION, "Block mutated: %s\n", state.ToString());
+        LogDebug(log, "Block mutated: %s\n", state.ToString());
```

where `m_log` / `log` types can vary and be defined by the subsystem. This allows subsystems to attach extra context to log messages like wallet names, or request ids. It also allows more than a single log stream to exist, and for messages to be logged to specified streams. Having a single global log stream works very well for `bitcoind` and will not change. But it limits functionality of libbitcoinkernel, forcing all potential users of the library, including applications written in different languages and running in different environments (like jupyter notebooks) to use shared global state and not be able to do things like get an isolated log trace from one operation.

The change is fully backwards compatible and does not require any updates to code that wants to continue using the macros as they are. The implementation of the macros is also improved. They now provide improved error messages when called with the wrong arguments. And they only call underlying `ShouldLog` `Log` and `Format` hooks as needed to avoid unnecessary work. The PR also adds more test coverage and documentation.

---

Note: Originally this PR also removed some restrictions around passing category constants to log macros to try to make them more consistent, but these changes were too controversial and have been dropped.

---

pulls.title: ipc: Expose Chain interface to IPC clients
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Processes connected to `bitcoin-node` over IPC (with `-ipcbind`) can use the `Mining` interface, but they can't currently use the `Chain` interface to read chain data or follow chain events. Chain data could be useful to third-party clients and Bitcoin Core's own wallet could use this as well to run in a separate process (#10102). But exposing all of `interfaces::Chain` to external clients would make its methods hard to change, since the wallet uses them as internal API (#34981).

**Solution:** Add capnp wrappers for `interfaces::Chain`, split into two interfaces backed by the same C++ class:

- `Chain`, returned by `Init.makeChain`, is stable. It follows Cap'n Proto schema evolution rules, so existing clients keep working as methods are added. It starts with the five block lookup methods: `findBlock`, `findFirstBlockWithTimeAndHeight`, `findAncestorByHeight`, `findAncestorByHash` and `findCommonAncestor`.
- `UnstableChain`, returned by `Init.makeUnstableChain`, extends `Chain` with every other method, for Bitcoin Core's internal C++ callers, such as the wallet, communicating over IPC. It can change in any way between releases. Incompatible changes renumber `makeUnstableChain`, so old clients get an error instead of calling the wrong methods.

Methods can move from `UnstableChain` to `Chain` once we're willing to support them for external use. `test/functional/interface_ipc.py` shows a Python client calling both interfaces. Like the existing IPC interfaces, these are only available to processes that can connect to the IPC socket, which already grants full node access through `Init.makeRpc`.

**Merge order:** This depends on bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#377 and a subtree update that includes it (this PR currently carries that subtree change as its first commit), and on #36520, which fixes node crashes IPC clients could trigger with invalid `Chain` arguments.

---

This PR is part of the [process separation project](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/28722).

pulls.title: addrman: apply time penalty in nTime check
pulls.body:
There is an existing check in `AddSingle()` that prevents us from increasing the `RefCount` of an address when the same announcement is received again from a different peer, which regularly happens with gossip relay - an addr can take different routes through the network to us.

However, the check is ineffective: when the entry was first added, its `nTime` was stored with a [2h time penalty](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/9d4325f40316d2c81d34418dc075b235173d0cec/src/net_processing.cpp#L6044) applied, so `addr.nTime > pinfo->nTime` holds even for an identical announcement. As a result, a single announcement relayed to us by several peers could increase an address's multiplicity in the new table, up to 8.

Fix this by applying the penalty in the comparison too, matching the `nTime` update check a few lines above.

This is just a small logic bugfix, it doesn't change things in adversarial scenarios, since peers can just do multiple announcements with changed `nTime` if they want to boost their `RefCount` artificially.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Contain all legacy wallet and migration related things in its own subdirectory, namespace, and classes
pulls.body:
Originally, legacy wallet migration was built upon the foundation of being able to load legacy wallets. Now that we no longer support loading legacy wallets, there is no reason to keep any of the legacy wallet loading and migration code in the main wallet objects. Having this co-mingling of never-to-be-changed legacy wallet code and new descriptor wallet code makes it difficult to implement new things into the wallet.

This PR fully separates out all of the legacy wallet related things into a subdirectory `wallet/legacy`, with everything in that directory under a `wallet::legacy_migration` namespace so as to prevent accidental usage outside of legacy wallets. This includes a little bit of duplication with current loading code, but not that much, and we are able to both remove unrelated descriptor wallet loading from the legacy wallet loading, and unrelated legacy wallet loading from normal descriptor wallet loading.

`LegacyWallet` is introduced as a subclass of `CWallet` which contains all of the relevant legacy wallet and migration functions so that `CWallet` cannot accidentally use some legacy wallet function. Additionally, `LegacyDataSPKM` is moved into a new file and this new namespace so that it cannot be used outside of migration.

Lastly, `ReorderTransactions` is a legacy wallet only function that is also moved into `LegacyWallet`.

Builds upon #34909, and depends on #36823 for removing some functions that were previously used by migration.

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
This is split off from #36521. This PR focuses on reducing memory usage of transactions in memory, leaving performance improvements for other PRs.

`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every non-empty element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization.

This PR first introduces encapsulation for `CScriptWitness`, hiding its representation. The last commit then changes the representation to be single `std::unique_ptr<byte[]>` which for non-empty witness stacks stores their serialization prefixed by a small length header. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place; they can only be replaced in their entirety. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead.

`CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes. Worst-case allocated size for transactions kept in memory drops from roughly 28 bytes/WU to 1.6 bytes/WU.

This worsens deserialization and validation time, adding some 50-70 ms per block to the worst case for me. I have follow-ups that instead improve the worst case deserialization time significantly. Other minor degradations:
* libbitcoinkernel's witness stack element accessor becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the index of the witness element; using it to iterate a whole witness may therefore become $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$.
* `CScriptWitness::back()` is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the length of the witness stack.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

pulls.title: CI: silent merge check
pulls.body:
In this design there is a new GHA job merged into the main repo that adds check runs to each PR on whether they have a silent merge conflict or not.

The idea is that we have a job that pretty much runs 24/7 triggered every 6 hours or so and set to run for 5.5 hours, it could be set to run on a GHA runner rather than a Cirrus runner. Obviously running on a Cirrus runner (or even multiple runners) would dramatically speed up how many PRs can be checked for silent merge conflicts.

The job uses the Github checks API to add a passing or failing test run to each PR directly. The silent merge check job itself should always pass, it writes pass or fail checks to the PRs.

It will look through all open PRs and discard anything that has a git merge failure or a failing test with the thinking that there is no point checking something that can't be merged anyway. Then it will select PRs that have not had a silent merge check and one by one pull the merge branch of the PR and the full CI job "Previous releases" on that branch.

When all PRs have been checked it will then re-check a PR that was checked the longest time ago.

pulls.title: net_processing: set fDisconnect instead of calling DisconnectNode
pulls.body: `MaybeDiscourageAndDisconnect` calls `DisconnectNode` which creates a `CSubNet` containing only the `CNode`'s address. This will disconnect every `CNode` with the same IP address. This is normally not a problem, except for clearnet-over-tor. If a node has an honest clearnet-over-tor inbound connection, the IP of the inbound peer will be the exit node's IP address. If an attacker connects to the node through the same exit node and sends an invalid message, they can cause every inbound peer sharing the exit node's IP to get disconnected. Fix this by only disconnecting the misbehaving `CNode` rather than every `CNode` sharing the IP.

pulls.title: net: stop monitoring select exceptions outside Windows
pulls.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
> 
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by ignoring the exceptionSet. Except on Windows, where we instead disconnect if its used.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

The PR makes two additional changes for clarity:
- wrap the `FD_ISSET` check in `#ifdef WIN32` (no behavior change)
- instead of `if (recvSet || errorSet)`, check `errorSet` separately and earlier (emits a different log message)

Test coverage is introduced in `p2p_socket_errors.py`.

Finally a similar fix is applied to HTTP.

pulls.title: net: option to disallow v1 connection on ipv4 and ipv6 peers
pulls.body:
resolves #29618.

This PR adds a config flag option `-v2onlyclearnet` which disallows outbound v1 connections on ipv4 and ipv6 networks since they're unencrypted. outbound v1 connections are still possible from tor/i2p/cjdns peers since they're encrypted networks.

- v1 outbound connections to peers are not attempted
- v1 reconnections are not attempted (if peer is falsely advertised as v2 peer and we attempt a v2 connection but it fails, we do not attempt a v1 reconnection when `-v2onlyclearnet` is switched on)

Currently 70% of reachable nodes in network supporting v2 (according to https://21.ninja/reachable-nodes/node-service-share/ and https://bitnodes.io/nodes). Also found 81% of addresses supporting v2 in the addrman of nodes I checked - personal node and the nodes in [peer.observer](https://peer.observer/addrman/alice). (You can use [this branch ](https://github.com/stratospher/bitcoin/commits/addrinfo_service_display/)to check the % of v2 addresses in a node's addrman.)

EDIT: see [summary](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30951#issuecomment-4346061700) on pros and cons for whether to allow v2 inbounds or not for `-v2onlyclearnet`.

pulls.title: scripted-diff: Type-safe settings retrieval
pulls.body:
This PR changes the way settings are registered and retrieved to provide more compile-time safety. Currently settings are [registered](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/03cff2c1421e5db59963eba1a845ef5dd318c275/src/init.cpp#L504) and [retrieved](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/03cff2c1421e5db59963eba1a845ef5dd318c275/src/init.cpp#L173) like:

```c++
// Register setting
argsman.AddArg("-pid=<file>", strprintf("Specify pid file. Relative paths will be prefixed by a net-specific datadir location. (default: %s)", BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME), ArgsManager::ALLOW_ANY, OptionsCategory::OPTIONS);

// Retrieve setting
args.GetPathArg("-pid", BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME)
```

But this is not ideal because nothing checks that setting names are spelled correctly, or that default values (`BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME`) are used consistently in the help string and retrieval sites, or that settings are retrieved with consistent types (bool, int, string, path, or list). This PR addresses these issues by adding setting [declarations](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init_settings.h#L267-L270) which allow settings to be [registered](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init.cpp#L484) and [retrieved](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init.cpp#L164C38-L164C59) like:

```c++
// Declare setting
using PidSetting = common::Setting<
    "-pid=<file>", fs::path, {.legacy = true},
    "Specify pid file. Relative paths will be prefixed by a net-specific datadir location. (default: %s)">
    ::DefaultFn<[] { return BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME; }>;

// Register setting
PidSetting::Register(argsman);

// Retrieve setting
PidSetting::Get(args)
```

---

#### Suggestions for review

All the real changes in this PR are in the last scripted-diff commit:

- [scripted-diff: Replace AddArgs / GetArgs calls with Setting Register / Get calls](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31260/commits/73c1f852eba2a48be0f03816a957e46ce6275bd9)

If you take a few minutes to look at the changes applied in this scripted-diff commit, you'll understand everything this PR is doing. A good place to start looking around in this commit is the generated [`src/init_settings.h`](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/pr/scripty/src/init_settings.h) file which declares the settings that get registered in [src/init.cpp](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/pr/scripty/src/init.cpp). Then you can look at the surrounding diffs and see they are just replacing `AddArg` and `GetArg` calls.

The other notable commit is second commit, which implements the `Setting` class:

- [common: Add Setting class to support typed Settings](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31260/commits/9c1cdb31eac5a180950dee0c6135918ce70b60f1)

The other commits do minor things like moving code or updating linters. The python script that implements the scripted diff is a temporary artifact that gets deleted. The python script is complicated because it does things like parsing c++ code to extract help strings, and figuring out the right types to declare settings with so code compiles. But the entire scope of the script is to (1) generate Setting type definitions, (2) add #includes, and (3) replace `AddArg()` calls with `Register()` calls and `GetArg()` calls with `Get()` calls. So there is not much the script can actually do wrong without triggering build and test failures.

---

#### Extensions

This PR only adds the ability to declare individual settings with built-in types. It doesn't provide any new runtime behavior, but a branch in issue #22978 extends the `Setting` class implemented here to support runtime setting validation, additional types like `std::variant`, additional conversion options, custom types, custom validation, and groups of settings declared as options structs.

This change is mostly orthogonal to #16545. #16545 only provides runtime type checking while this PR only provides compile-time checking with no new runtime behavior. But this change does allow a nicer way of declaring types in #16545, using c++ types like `int` instead of flags like `ALLOW_INT`, or`std::vector<std::string>` instead of `ALLOW_STRING | ALLOW_LIST`.

pulls.title: net: add -outboundbind option for outgoing source address
pulls.body:
Closes #6476

Adds `-outboundbind=<addr>` to set the source address of outgoing clearnet
connections, one per address family. It is separate from `-bind`; without it,
outbound follows the OS routing table as before.

- The command line wins over the config file, as for other options.
- Clearnet only: Tor and I2P use their own transport, CJDNS is direct but not
  IPv4/IPv6, and a proxy leaves the option inert for that family (with a
  startup warning).
- The effective address per family is trial-bound at startup, like `-bind` via
  `BindListenPort`; a port, the wildcard, or a non-clearnet value is rejected. A
  failed bind at connect time aborts the connection, with no fallback.

Functional and unit tests cover both families, the startup rejections, and the
bind-before-connect path.

Based on vasild's approach in
https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/6476#issuecomment-1666472338.

{

}

Citating @supertestnet

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization, while becoming very slow to deserialize.

This PR stores the stack as its serialization in a single allocation (or none if the stack is empty), with a small header holding its size and the offset of the last element. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place, only allowing replacing them entirely. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead. `CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes.

Later commits also introduce stricter checking during deserialization, rejecting the following before fully deserializing:
* Transactions with more inputs/outputs than are possible in a valid transaction.
* Transactions with 0 inputs or 0 outputs (applied in P2P, but not RPC etc. for backward compatibility).
* Transactions/blocks that exceed the 4M weight limit (also only applied in P2P).

The result is a significant reduction in the worst-case time and memory allocations needed for deserialization, both in valid and invalid transactions. With it, the worst-case memory of a valid deserialized block drops from 106.8 MiB to 6.0 MiB. Memory usage during deserialization can temporarily be higher: up to 7.8 MiB for valid blocks, and up to 13.4 MiB for invalid blocks, which can combine a few temporary vector allocations of up to 5 MB each.

Deserialization time and memory of the deserialized block, master → PR. Runtimes are medians in milliseconds. Memory usage is in MiB, and ✕ means rejected at deserialization time. Peak memory refers to the memory during deserialization itself, not persisted in the deserialized `CBlock` object. Numbers over 50 ms, 20 MiB usage, or 100 MiB peak are in **bold**.

| block | gcc | clang | mem | peak mem |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Valid blocks** |
| 1 tx, max 1-byte wit elems | **99.1** → 16.0 | **111.4** → 21.9 | **106.8** → 3.8 | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, max empty wit elems | **279.2** → 18.7 | **293.7** → 25.1 | **91.5** → 3.8 | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout, 1-item wit | 12.33 → 13.39 | 15.00 → 15.43 | 6.7 → 6.0 | 6.7 → 6.0 |
| max txs, 1 txin and 1 txout | 6.43 → 7.04 | 7.87 → 8.30 | 5.8 → 5.6 | 5.8 → 5.6 |
| 1 tx, max txins, 1-elem wit | 4.53 → 4.68 | 5.04 → 5.37 | 4.0 → 2.9 | 4.0 → 2.9 |
| mainnet block 969729 | 5.30 → 5.47 | 5.97 → 6.20 | 3.5 → 2.9 | 3.5 → 2.9 |
| **Invalid blocks** |
| 400k txs, many wit elems, truncated | **84.8** → 16.1 | **95.6** → 21.8 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 12.6 |
| 400k txs, big wit+scriptsig, truncated | **84.0** → 16.1 | **96.0** → 21.7 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 13.4 |
| 1 tx, 2M 1-byte wit elems | **98.0** → 10.6 | **109.9** → 16.2 | **106.8** → ✕ | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, 4M empty wit elems | **271.0** → 13.4 | **288.9** → 19.6 | **91.6** → ✕ | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max empty txs | **101.0** → 0.006 | **139.0** → 0.008 | **67.1** → ✕ | 67.1 → 4.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout | 27.6 → 7.3 | 34.5 → 8.5 | **23.4** → ✕ | 23.4 → 6.4 |

So in addition to improving worst cases very significantly, it also provides modest memory usage improvements to the common case. This translates to mildly increasing the effective capacity of memory-bounded data structures that store transactions, like the mempool.

Some notable changes:
* By implementing some checks (for inherently consensus-invalid things) in the deserialization logic, behavior may change. In particular, deserialization errors in P2P cause messages to be dropped/ignored, rather than triggering validation or net processing logic (which may include disconnections and/or inserting into reject filters).
* The rejection of transactions with too many inputs or outputs applies everywhere, including in RPC. That's hopefully a desirable change, but a change in behavior still.
* Random access to the witness stack elements becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$. This is not a problem for any validation logic, but may be relevant for the libbitcoinkernel API which exposes an individual element accessor.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

There are a few possible follow-ups:
* Enforce the 400k WU policy limit during transaction deserialization when active (instead of the 4M WU consensus limit).
* Extend this approach to entire `CTransaction`, allowing all transaction data to be stored packed together in a few allocations (rather than one per input, one per output, one per witness) plus some index structure to access it efficiently. That's a much bigger change, needing abstractions like #35569, but would reduce the maximum memory usage per WU for valid blocks from around 1.5 bytes/WU to 1.1 bytes/WU (compared to ~28 bytes/WU in master).

pulls.body:
Follow up suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36791#discussion_r4568050151.

`waitNext` measures its timeout and 1-second fee tick with the wall clock, while `waitTipChanged` uses the steady clock. This means a wall clock jump changes how long `waitNext` waits, and it never times out while mocktime is frozen.

Use the steady clock for the deadline and tick. `NodeClock` is kept only for the testnet 20-minute rule, which must compare node time with the tip's timestamp.

pulls.title: wallet: allow skipping script paths
pulls.body:
While testing MuSig2 integration in #29675 I ran into a Ledger bug https://github.com/LedgerHQ/app-bitcoin-new/issues/329 that was triggered because we signed for a script path in addition to the key path. The bug itself will be fixed, but it seems useful in general to be able to skip script path signing (and finalizing).

For example, you may have a 2-of-2 musig() descriptor with some sort of fallback after coins are N blocks old. For both on chain privacy and fee reasons, you don't want to use this path unless absolutely necessary. But our wallet can't know if our co-signer still has their key, so we sign the script path at all times. This could lead to accidental broadcast.

This PR introduces a `keypath_only` option (default `false` for now) to the following RPC methods:
- `send` 
- `sendall`
- `walletcreatefundedpsbt`
- `walletprocesspsbt`
- `descriptorprocesspsbt`

The resulting PSBT won't _add_ `taproot_scripts` or `taproot_script_path_sigs`. It does still have `taproot_bip32_derivs` and `musig2_participant_pubkeys`.

It will not remove `taproot_scripts` from an existing PSBT, but it won't add a corresponding entry to `taproot_script_path_sigs`. We also won't finalize a PSBT without keypath spend, even with complete script paths. This protects against other participants accidentally including them.

The `wallet_taproot.py` tests are expanded to cover this behavior.

It can also be tested with https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/pull/91.

pulls.title: util: Add and use AssertUnreachable
pulls.body:
The current code uses assertions with falsy literal values in a few places. This is perfectly fine, but this comes with a bit of confusion sometimes:

* `assert(false)` may cause confusion when it is unclear if `NDEBUG` can disable it. (The intention is to disallow `NDEBUG` compilation). Also, it can lead to warnings when used with clang-cl.exe (GCC seems to understand it)
* `Assert(false)` hides the noreturn attribute behind a function call, which may cause GCC return-type warnings. (Clang seems to understand it)

See https://godbolt.org/z/h7PT3jh3Y for the clang-cl/GCC warning reproducer.

* When C++23 will be allowed, devs may prefer `std::unreachable`. However, this is unsafe and will invoke UB.
* There is confusion why a `CHECK_NONFATAL` macro exists, but no fatal equivalent.

Fix all those issues by:

* Adding a new `AssertUnreachable`, which directly calls the noreturn `assertion_fail` helper.
* Adding an `assert_falsy` linter to enforce code to use this macro.

pulls.title: i2p: pass base32 address directly to stream connect
pulls.body:
As the SAM protocol accepts a `.b32.i2p` address as the `DESTINATION` parameter for the `STREAM CONNECT` command, the `NAMING LOOKUP` round trip can be skipped on every outbound connection.

This should ostensibly make failure handling more accurate in certain situations as well, since a peer that cannot be resolved now returns `CANT_REACH_PEER`/`TIMEOUT` rather than there being an empty `VALUE=` key in the lookup reply. A missing `VALUE=` is a proxy error, so the attempt isn't recorded in AddrMan.

Router implementation versions that support this (Java I2P 0.9.48, i2pd 2.38.0) are older than ones supporting `i2cp.leaseSetEncType=6,4` (see #35696), so there should be no compatibility issues here.

Source:
https://i2p.net/en/docs/api/samv3/#sam-virtual-streams-connect

pulls.title: Interfaces: Expose UTXO Snapshot Loading and Add Progress Notifications
pulls.body:
# Add UTXO Snapshot Loading Interface and Progress Notifications

This PR implements a complete interface for loading UTXO snapshots through the GUI, including progress notifications to provide user feedback during the loading process.

---

## Changes

### Commit 1: interfaces: expose UTXO snapshot functionality (loading/activate) in node interface

- Added a new virtual method `snapshot` to the node interface for loading UTXO snapshots from a path.
- Added `snapshot.h` to `src/interfaces` defining the Snapshot interface; `activate()` returns `util::Result<const CBlockIndex*>` to   carry either the base block index on success or a descriptive error message on failure, matching the shape of `ChainstateManager::ActivateSnapshot()`.
- Added a `getMetadata` accessor so callers can read snapshot metadata populated during activation without re-parsing the file.
- Added `SnapshotImpl` in src/node/interfaces.cpp: opens the snapshot file, parses metadata, and forwards to `ChainstateManager::ActivateSnapshot()`, propagating any error as util::Error{...}.

This change enhances the user's ability to load UTXO snapshots through the GUI and/or RPC.

### Commit 2: `notifications: Implement snapshot load progress notifications`

- Added a new signal `SnapshotLoadProgress` for snapshot load progress in the UI interface.
- Updated the notifications interface to include a method for reporting snapshot loading progress.
- Enhanced the `ChainstateManager` to report progress during snapshot loading.
- Implemented the necessary handler in the kernel notifications to relay progress updates.

This change improves user feedback during the snapshot loading process.

### Commit 3: `rpc: refactor loadtxoutset to use snapshot interface`

- Updated the `loadtxoutset` RPC to call the new snapshot interface instead of directly working with chainstate internals. File opening, metadata parsing, and activation now all happen inside `interfaces::Snapshot::activate()` rather than being split between the RPC handler and the interface.
- Removed the redundant pre-parse block in the RPC handler; its file-open and metadata-parse work duplicated what activate() already performs.
- Collapsed the RPC error handling to a single `RPC_INTERNAL_ERROR` built from `util::ErrorString(activation_result).original`, using the `"Unable to load UTXO snapshot: %s. (%s)"` format established in #30267 / #30395.
- Read `coins_loaded` from `snapshot->getMetadata()` after `activate()` populates it.
- Updated `feature_assumeutxo.py` to assert on the unified error code for file-open and metadata-parse failures (message substrings unchanged).
Improves modularity by consolidating snapshot handling through the interface layer.
---

## Technical Details

The implementation includes:

- **UI Interface Enhancement**
  Added `SnapshotLoadProgress` signal to `CClientUIInterface` with corresponding signal declaration and implementation.

- **Node Interface**
  Added `loadSnapshot` virtual method to the node interface with implementation in `interfaces.cpp`.

- **Progress Notifications**
  Implemented `snapshotLoadProgress` method in `KernelNotifications` class to relay progress updates to the UI.

- **Base Interface**
  Added `snapshotLoadProgress` virtual method to the kernel notifications interface.

---

## Benefits

- **User Experience**
  Provides real-time feedback during UTXO snapshot loading operations.

- **GUI Integration**
  Enables loading UTXO snapshots directly through the Bitcoin Core GUI.

- **Progress Tracking**
  Users can monitor the progress of snapshot loading operations.

- **Consistent Interface**
  Follows the existing pattern for progress notifications in the codebase.

## Testing

- **Daemon** build and launch `bitcoind` then with `bitcoin-cli` load a snapshot using:
```bash
./bitcoin-cli -rpcclienttimeout=0 -signet loadtxoutset /path/to/utxo-snapsshot.dat
```
- **QT Widgets**: build and run [this](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/gui/pull/870) draft PR in legacy gui repo 
- **QML** version: for a modern look build and run [this](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/gui-qml/pull/488) PR in the newly updated gui-qml repo

pulls.title: blocks: add resumable reobfuscation for existing block files
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Nodes that synced before v28 may store block and undo files effectively unobfuscated with a zero XOR key. There is no built-in way to obfuscate those existing files, rotate their key, or deliberately replace it with a zero key without resyncing.

**Fix:** Add `-reobfuscate-blocks[=<value>]` to rewrite existing `blk*.dat` and `rev*.dat` files before chainstate loading. With no value or `=1`, the option generates a random 8-byte key. A 16-character hexadecimal value selects an exact key, including all zeros to remove obfuscation, while malformed values fail during startup. If the selected key is already active, block and undo files are left unchanged.

Files are rewritten in fixed-size chunks, staged with a `.reobfuscated` suffix, committed before the originals are removed, and renamed to their original names after all rewrites finish. The target key is staged as `xor.dat.reobfuscated`, which is also used to resume an interrupted migration. Progress is reported in the log and through kernel notifications marked as resumable.

**Benchmark:** The migration is single-threaded and processes one file at a time.

|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Apple M4 Max laptop | SSD | ~955k | ~854 GB | 11,232 | 10.18 | 93,804 |
| Intel Core i9 | SSD | ~909k | ~725 GB | 10,238 | 23.1 | 39,351 |

pulls.title: mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.


I analyzed the reason=expiry evictions from a 15-node monitoring fleet (data courtesy of b10c) and checked what happened to each transaction afterwards.

Across 938,157 unique expired transactions (2024-02-16 to 2026-10-21):

- 92.0% (863,451) were later mined; only 8.0% (74,706) never confirmed.
- At least 34% (316,381) show rebroadcast evidence, and 87% of those confirmed.
- Of the ones that confirm, half are mined within about 5 days of first expiry and 90% within about 55 days.

So time-based expiry is evicting transactions that get mined anyway, usually after a rebroadcast, it costs relay bandwidth.

See thread https://bnoc.xyz/t/request-how-many-mempool-transactions-are-evicted-by-time/132

pulls.body:
**Problem:** Block index ordering is used by chain selection and `CheckBlockIndex()`. The work comparator is defined out of line and can compare the same chain work twice.

pulls.title: wallet: make migration more robust against failures
pulls.body:
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process. 
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention. 
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.

This replaces the FreeBSD cross-compilation job with a native build and test job inside a FreeBSD VM. NetBSD and OpenBSD retain their existing cross-compilation jobs.

We currently cross-compile BSD binaries without testing them in this repository. Running tests before merge should help catch platform-specific regressions that would otherwise first appear in nightly builds. This starts with FreeBSD because it has been the most reliable BSD platform in the nightly jobs.

As we don't have native FreeBSD runners, the job uses [vmactions/freebsd-vm](https://github.com/vmactions/freebsd-vm), which is also used by the nightly builds. It reuses the existing CI scripts, depends build, and cache actions where possible.

The VM image is cached after its `prepare` step installs dependencies. The job also restores and saves the usual build caches. Initial testing on free GitHub Actions runners took approximately 60 minutes without caches and 20–30 minutes with caches populated. Performance on Warp runners remains untested.

The VM uses the runner's available CPU count and 75% of its RAM, leaving the remaining memory for the host and VM overhead. There is some overhead after testing while `rsync` copies cache directories back out of the VM.

The patchset also suppresses `lsof` warnings on FreeBSD that would otherwise interfere with functional tests.

Two functional tests are currently excluded:

- `feature_reindex_init` failed during testing.
- `p2p_private_broadcast_retry_v1` took an unusually long time.

Both warrant further investigation.

The job requires enabling one additional action:

```text
vmactions/freebsd-vm@v1
```

pulls.title: net: validate Tor onion service replies and cached keys
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A node creates its onion service through Tor's control protocol and caches the returned `PrivateKey` value for reconnects.
Tor reply parsing unescapes quoted values, so a control endpoint can return a value containing a line break or space.
On reconnect, the node inserts that value unquoted into an `ADD_ONION` command.
CRLF frames the remainder as a separate command, while a space adds further arguments.
An unprivileged local process can exploit this by impersonating the default loopback endpoint while Tor is unavailable, seeding the cache, and releasing the port before Tor is available again.
A compromised operator-configured endpoint can return the same malicious value.
The reply handler also continues after receiving an invalid service ID, logging it and caching the key before attempting to advertise the invalid address.
A later reply without a service ID can reuse an ID left by an earlier reply.

**Fix:** This PR validates the returned service ID as a Tor v3 onion address before logging it, caching the key, or advertising the service.
Each reply must provide its own service ID, and reply fields stay local until validation succeeds.
Key validation accepts `NEW:ED25519-V3` or an `ED25519-V3` key whose Base64 payload decodes to 64 bytes.
Returned keys are validated before adoption or caching, and cached keys are validated before reuse.
A malformed cached key leaves the onion service unavailable until the operator removes the file and restarts the node. It cannot inject another command or argument.

pulls.title: mining: add getMemoryLoad() and track template non-mempool memory footprint
pulls.body:
IPC clients can hold block templates indefinitely, keeping transactions alive after they leave the mempool. This adds `getMemoryLoad()` to estimate the memory held on behalf of all mining clients, as discussed in bitcoin/bitcoin#33899. It does not impose a limit.

The estimate includes each tracked template's vectors and the transactions it references that are no longer in the mempool. Transaction objects shared by multiple templates are counted once. Dummy coinbase transactions and the template cached by the `getblocktemplate` RPC are excluded.

`BlockTemplateManager` tracks templates through weak references, so the registry does not prolong their lifetime. Templates unregister when destroyed, including when IPC cleanup happens after shutdown has reset the manager. Clients can reduce the reported memory load by releasing stale templates or explicitly calling `destroy()`.

The result is an estimate: the mempool can change during calculation, and eviction followed by re-entry as a different transaction object can cause undercounting.

Example client usage: [stratum-mining/sv2-tp#63](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-tp/pull/63).

- `refactor: pass block template by reference to WaitAndCreateNewBlock`
- `refactor: share ownership of BlockTemplateManager`
- `mining: track block templates held by IPC clients`
- `mining: add GetTemplateMemoryUsage()`

pulls.title: [DO NOT MERGE] Erlay: bandwidth-efficient transaction relay protocol (Full implementation)
pulls.body:
Erlay Project Tracking: [#30249](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/30249)
Conceptual Discussion: [#34542](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34542)

---

This is a full implementation of Erlay. Its purpose is to check the integrity and correctness of the implementation against changes/additions that may originate from the review process and/or rebases on top of newer functionality.

This is not to be merged. Functionality will be spread across multiple smaller PRs to ease the review process.

---
## Approach

This approach uses Erlay as a fallback mechanism for transaction propagation. Instead of mixing fanout and reconciliation into a single connection type, the current approach leaves the existing connections as they are, and adds additional low-bandwidth connections to be used in case the node is being eclipsed. This connections should have minimal cost under normal circumstances, and only undergo real traffic in case other 8 full-outbound connections are being captured.

## outbound-full-reconciliation connections

For now, we are adding 4 additional reconciliation-only connections to the node while we test it's impact on real node running the approach. Further analysis may be needed to pick a meaningful value for this. The number of inbound connections should also be scaled based on how many connections we are adding.

pulls.title: mining: add TxCollection to bandwidth-efficiently validate external block templates
pulls.body:
The Stratum v2 spec defines a [Job Declarator Server](https://stratumprotocol.org/specification/06-job-declaration-protocol) (JDS), whose job it is to approve custom miner templates. Since #34020 it can use `getTransactionsByWitnessID()` to request transactions from the node, instead of maintaining its own mempool mirror (see https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-apps/pull/911), and then request any missing transactions from the miner.

The new `TxCollection` interface introduced by this PR optimizes this further. We build and validate the block template ourselves now, based on the requested transaction list and our own mempool, so known transactions don't need to cross the IPC boundary. This also fits the [draft spec](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-spec/discussions/239) for JDS custom job validation through a Template Provider.

The following flow is demonstrated in https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-apps/pull/599:

1. Miner generates a template, e.g. using our `createNewBlock()` IPC method
2. They send the list of `Wtxid`s to the pool's JDS
3. JDS calls `Mining::collectTxs()` (this PR) with that `Wtxid` list
4. We check the list against our mempool and hold a `CTransactionRef` for each match
5. The JDS queries `unknownTxPos()` to learn what's missing from the collection
6. The JDS requests the fully serialized missing transactions from the miner (using native Stratum v2 messages)
7. JDS calls `addMissingTxs()` which completes the collection
8. JDS calls `makeTemplate()` which reconstructs the block and validates it, optionally with the coinbase it intends to use (e.g. to check the reward amount); a node-generated dummy is used otherwise. The JDS needs the check to succeed, may relay the BIP-22 failure reason to the miner.
9. It returns a `BlockTemplate` which works as if we generated the template ourselves, but with methods like `waitNext()` disabled. The JDS can call `submitSolution()` (the sv2 spec allows for redundant block reconstruction by both the miner node and the JDS).

If this sounds very similar to compact block relay: it is! In fact, it would be easy to expand the above methods to take transaction short ids instead of `Wtxid`. That may be useful for the [p2pool revival project](https://www.vinteum.org/blog/reviving-p2pool-welcoming-johnny-santos-as-a-vinteum-grantee), which needs a way to validate and relay weak blocks as compact blocks. pulls.title: rpc: handle malformed jsonrpc 2.0 requests correctly
pulls.body:
While reviewing #36642 I found something else we missed in JSON-RPC 2.0:

If we receive a malformed request we would assume that we couldn't parse it's jsonrpc version and send an HTTP error.  This is how the legacy jsonrpc server worked (despite that behavior not ever being part of any ratified jsonrpc spec) and we maintain it as Bitcoin "legacy" jsonrpc protocol. However it's possible to form a request that does properly indicate jsonrpc 2.0 but is still malformed. In that case, we should not send an HTTP error: the correct protocol is to respond with `HTTP 200 OK` and include the jsonrpc error message in the response.

The solution is to check if we know the request's jsonrpc version before responding with an error.

We already correctly handle such malformed requests in batches and this is already tested in `test_batch_requests()` in `interface_rpc.py`

On master, the functional test in this PR actually crashes the node because the assumption is codified. Note that this crash requires:
1. RPC Authentication
2. A debug build

So this is not an urgent security fix, but a bug that might disrupt testing.

```
node0 stderr httprpc.cpp:46
    UniValue JSONErrorReply(UniValue, const JSONRPCRequest &, HTTPStatusCode &):
        'jreq.m_json_version != JSONRPCVersion::V2' check failed.
```


In release builds the node doesn't crash, but it returns HTTP 400 with a JSON-RPC 2.0 error body instead of HTTP 200.

pulls.title: mining: move getblocktemplate cache into BlockTemplateManager
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #35675. This addresses the `getblocktemplate` part of the "Remove remaining global states" TODO in #33758, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35675#pullrequestreview-5299625960.

`getblocktemplate` reuses its last template until the tip changes, or until the mempool changes and the template is more than 5 seconds old. That cache currently lives in four function-local statics, which:

- live as long as the process, so the cached `CBlockIndex*` can outlive its `ChainstateManager` (as in unit tests);
- rely on `cs_main` being held, which nothing checks;
- can't be unit tested.

This PR moves the cache into `BlockTemplateManager`, in three commits:

1. **rpc:** refactors the statics in place into a `CachedBlockTemplate` struct and a `GetNewOrCachedBlockTemplate()` helper, `GUARDED_BY(::cs_main)`. The template's `hashPrevBlock` replaces the cached `CBlockIndex*`, and the 5 seconds becomes `GBT_TEMPLATE_REBUILD_INTERVAL`.
2. **refactor:** moves them into `BlockTemplateManager`. It's easiest to review with `git show --color-moved=dimmed-zebra --color-moved-ws=allow-indentation-change`.
3. **test:** adds a unit test for each rebuild rule and for the retry after a failed build.

No behavior change is intended, and only `getblocktemplate` uses the cache. It uses `cs_main` rather than its own mutex, since the RPC already holds it and building a template takes it anyway.

pulls.title: [Demo] validation: remove AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Draft demo:** this is meant to showcase what complete AssumeUTXO removal could look like and the simplifications that AssumeUTXO currently prevents.
The decision about complete removal is of course still open. This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

**Smaller PRs:** I will carve out individual changes to gauge interest in each part, and link them here as they are opened.
Some of the findings are useful even if snapshot loading or background validation stays.
Feedback on which parts seem worth pursuing, and in which order, is welcome.

**Motivation:** this follows our in-person discussion at the October 2026 Core Dev meeting.
My impression was that there was rough agreement about the ambiguity background validation introduces: we trust a snapshot enough to use it immediately, but describe that trust as temporary until the same node finishes checking history.

Multiple chainstates affect much more than snapshot loading: ordinary validation changes have to account for different chainstate roles, candidate sets, notifications, downloads, pruning, cache allocation, database lifetimes and locks.
I am not sure this amount of complexity in the most critical part of our codebase is still worth it, given that adoption [isn't where we hoped it would be](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35054#issuecomment-4468360424).
Ordinary IBD is also getting faster: #35295 is already merged, and the upcoming `pruneassumevalid` will make pruned IBD even faster.

Snapshot bootstrapping without background validation can still offer an advantage: a new node becomes usable before ordinary IBD would finish because snapshot loading time scales with the UTXO set size, while ordinary IBD time scales with the blockchain size.
Whether that is worth its maintenance cost is a fair question, and we can discuss it here or in the dedicated PR where I will propose the removal.
Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.
This demo makes that cost, and the code we could remove, visible for that discussion.

**Background validation can be considered separately:** if we keep snapshot loading, I would prefer making its trust assumption explicit and distributing verification across ordinary IBD nodes, as proposed in #32377 and #36543.
That could give us wider independent checking of the commitment without making every snapshot user maintain a second chainstate.

Users who want to validate history themselves and transition to an archival node could rebuild with `-reindex` and pruning disabled.
Alternatively, they could run IBD in a separate datadir while their snapshot node remains usable, then switch once it is ready.
@Sjors's #36557 discusses dropping mandatory background sync and these alternatives.

**What the series demonstrates:**

* After the fixture cleanup in #36601, the next eight commits remove background validation while snapshot loading keeps working, a stopping point that can be reviewed on its own.
* The middle commits remove snapshot imports and startup resumption, then the validation, block storage, notification and release-process special cases they needed.
* The final seven commits add the simplifications this removal enables: startup in one pass, stable database ownership, one download path, a single prune height, and removal of the locks and diagnostics used to select and identify chainstates.

Ordinary validation, `-assumevalid`, pruning, `ChainstateManager` and UTXO export (`dumptxoutset`) remain.

**Related work:**

* [AJ's recent faster-loader branch](https://github.com/ajtowns/bitcoin/tree/202610-loadtxoutset-speedy) and [Sjors's chunked-import experiments](https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/tree/2026/10/utxo-coin-chunks) explore reducing import overhead while retaining snapshot support.
* #35054 contains the broader discussion about P2P snapshot distribution, its users and its costs.

pulls.title: wallet: skip APS when no partial spend exists
pulls.body:
Fixes #25150

APS (Avoid Partial Spends) runs a second coin selection pass that spends many
(possibly all) or none of the UTXOs sharing a scriptPubKey. The second pass runs
even when the first selection left no partial spend for it to avoid, and
aps_create_tx_internal then reports APS as used whenever the grouped result is
taken, overreporting how often a partial spend was avoided.

Detect partial spends by comparing selected vs available UTXO counts per
scriptPubKey, reusing the coins already fetched for selection and counting
manually selected inputs towards their scriptPubKey. Skip APS if none found.

Functional tests cover APS being skipped and a manually selected input making
the spend partial.

---

*Supersedes #34362.*

pulls.title: refactor: Add [[nodiscard]] to functions returning bool+mutable ref
pulls.body:
Legacy code often used a function signature of the form `bool Get...(const& in, mut& in_out);` to implement a getter that optionally returns a value.

In modern code, this can be replaced by `std::optional<_> Get...(const& in);`.

However, some legacy code remains. To ensure that the "imaginary optional" is not unwrapped when the getter returns false, add a C++17 `[[nodiscard]]` attribute to all those legacy functions.

There were only a few places that ignored the return value. I've fixed them in separate commits.

This should be easy to review via `--word-diff-regex=.` and then confirming that the attribute was added to such a getter.

pulls.title: contrib: ci: Monitor Windows signing certificate expiry
pulls.body:
Currently we have no automation in place to check that our code signing certificates are not expired or close to expiry. We have previously "relied on Release Candidates" as a dry-run for codesigners to realise that a certificate has expired and have time to fix it. "Noticing during RC cycle" also might not be appropriate in the future if we release more bugfix minor/patch releases on short notice.

In place of this process we can run a weekly CI job which will check the certificate's validity and open an issue when it passes an expiry threshold.

In this draft we only check the windows cert (as I couldn't find a mac one) and we set the alert threshold to 90 days.

When the threshold is passed, the job will open an issue in this repo (optionally tagging relevant key-holders).

pulls.title: rpc: Manual prune lock management (Take 2)
pulls.body:
This is a refreshed version of #19463, which was closed due to inactivity.

Motivation: On pruned nodes, if a wallet is not loaded while the node is running, blocks necessary for rescanning when the wallet is loaded may be pruned. This PR allows users and external wallet software to manually manage prune locks via RPC, so they can protect blocks needed for future rescans and also clean up locks that are no longer relevant (e.g. after permanently unloading a wallet from a node). This is useful both for Bitcoin Core's own wallet and for external wallets that use Bitcoin Core as a backend. Usage of temporary prune locking may also be helpful in other functional test scenarios but I didn't spend time to check where might apply.

This PR leverages the existing prune locks system we already have. The interface of the RPCs of the old PR has been slightly updated, it now matches the pattern used by `setban`/`listbanned` exactly. The locks are prefixed to distinguish them from the systems locks and prevent naming colissions. They are not persisted across restarts.

pulls.body:
Part of #36692: This splits it into one test case per policy rule, each building its own transaction.

The first commit replaces `g_dust` and `g_bare_multi` globals by a `StandardPolicy` struct, which defaults to the node defaults and is passed to each check,  e.g. `CheckIsStandard(t, {.max_op_return_relay = 83})`, so no case changes policy for another. 

Second commit splits `test_IsStandard` into independent test cases i.e. one test case per policy rule. Each starts from its own standard transaction built by a new `MakeTx` helper. Since transactions are no longer carried over between checks, some values that are irrelevant to the rule under test differ from before.

Third commit builds `IsStandard` test transactions declaratively. Each check constructs its transaction in one expression instead of mutating a shared one. `CheckDustThreshold` helper also deduplicates repeated "not dust at the threshold, dust one satoshi below" from test cases.

pulls.title: wallet: Fix detection of symlinks on Windows
pulls.body:
This PR implements symlink detection for Windows, since GCC [doesn't support symlinks on Windows](https://gcc.gnu.org/git/?p=gcc.git;a=blob;f=libstdc%2B%2B-v3/src/filesystem/ops-common.h;h=ba377905a2e90f7baf30c900b090f1f732397e08;hb=refs/heads/releases/gcc-13#l124). This is used by the wallet's `ListDatabases` in order to detect symlinks and avoid recursing them. It's also used in wallet path validation since that is also checking whether paths are symlinks, and we should properly detect symlinks on Windows.

Under the hood, the `IsSymlink` function uses `std::filesystem::is_symlink` for non-Windows systems. On Windows, it checks a file's attributes to determine if it is a [reparse point](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/reparse-points). Strictly speaking, this will also catch files that aren't symlinks, such as directories that are Onedrive mounts. I think it's fine to not be recursively searching such directories.

This is based on #34418 for the multiwallet test and CI changes that it enables. The last commit also removes the skipping of the symlink checks so that we are testing that the symlink handling behavior on Windows matches that on Linux and MacOS.

pulls.title: net: require a dedicated bind for automatic Tor
pulls.body:
**Problem:** When the automatic onion service has no dedicated `-bind=<addr>=onion`, Tor forwards incoming connections to the first normal P2P bind. A wildcard onion bind also fails to identify incoming Tor connections. In either case, network classification is incorrect and Tor peers may inherit permissions granted to the Tor daemon's IP address.

**Fix:** Refuse startup when `-listenonion` is enabled and an explicit `-bind` configuration lacks a dedicated, non-wildcard onion bind or includes a wildcard onion bind, following [the recommendation in #34892](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34892#issuecomment-5541662236). Users should add a specific `-bind=<addr>=onion` or set `-listenonion=0`.

Because `-listenonion` is enabled by default when listening, existing configurations with only a normal `-bind` must also be updated. Nodes without explicit `-bind` options retain the default dedicated onion listener.
